[MUQATIL:55:74-78/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The Lord's name is blessed; majesty means greatness and honor means generosity—none is more generous—and God praises Himself.
[TAB-FULL:v22p278#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The author glosses Dhu al-jalal as majesty; Ibn Abbas’s report expands this as majesty and greatness.
[TAB-FULL:v22p278#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses Dhu al-Jalal wa-al-Ikram as the possessor of majesty and greatness.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p105/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The surah closes by declaring what is fitting for God: that He be glorified and magnified.
[NAHHAS:v4p317/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Blessing in God's name means the persistence and stability of favor; the verse urges abundant invocation and supplication by His name with reverence and exaltation.
[NAHHAS:v4p317/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | ذي الجلال والإكرام means the Majestic and Generous.
[NAHHAS:v4p317/r12] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | A hadith recommends persistently invoking God as ذا الجلال والإكرام.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p253/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn ʿĀmir alone reads dhū al-jalāli with nominative wāw.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p253/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الجميع | reports | All readers also have the genitive dhī al-jalāli; codices are reported with variant spellings in the regions named.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p253/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The genitive makes dhī an adjective of rabbika, supported by Ibn Masʿūd’s codex, which has the genitive in both clauses.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p253/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī says jalāl is used only of God, supporting the genitive; the author counters with a poem applying jalāl to someone else.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p253/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | The nominative can be parsed by treating the word as a new nominal subject.
[SULAMI:v2p298/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | They gloss God's blessedness as exaltation and transcendence above the false claims of unbelievers; every creature's praise is limited by its own capacity and understanding.
[SULAMI:v2p298/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Human praise and knowledge cannot reach God, who exceeds human imagination; even the Prophet says no one can enumerate His praise, and He alone praises Himself fully.
[SULAMI:v2p298/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet's supplication says he cannot enumerate God's praise, for God is as He has praised Himself.
[THALABI:v9p198/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكرة | reports | Abu Bakra reports that the Prophet's recitation joined the phrases with waw, including rafraf khudr wa-abqariyy hissan and the final doxology; this is the Syrian reading in their codices.
[THALABI:v9p198/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The Syrian reading has ذو in the nominative in the final phrase, while the other readers have ذي in the genitive.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p206/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عامر | reports | He reads “dhu al-jalal” in the nominative, making it agree with “name”; this indicates that the name is the named one, since majesty is God’s attribute, not an attribute of naming.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:55:76-78/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The surah closes with words fitting to glorify and exalt God.
[DAMGHANI:v1p246/r4] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Ism can mean the named one itself: “the name of your Lord” means your Lord.
[JISHUMI:v9p6732#2/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn ʿĀmir reads “dhū al-jalāl” in the nominative as an adjective of “name,” matching the Syrian codices.
[JISHUMI:v9p6732#2/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قراءة الباقين | reports | The other readers use the genitive “dhī al-jalāl,” making it an adjective of the Lord, as in their codices.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p459#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · أهل الشام | reports | The Syrian readers recite dhū al-jalāl with nominative wāw, as in their codices, agreeing it with the divine name.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p459#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · عائشة | reports | ʿĀʾisha reports that after prayer the Prophet would sit only long enough to say that God is Peace, from Him comes peace, and He is blessed, Possessor of Majesty and Honor.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p236#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | In this location, الاسم is intended to refer to the named entity itself.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p236#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Calling upon God with the two names جلال and إكرام is meritorious and likely to be answered; the Prophet urges frequent use of the invocation يا ذا الجلال والإكرام.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p236#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الناس | reports | The majority read ذي الجلال in the genitive, agreeing with الرب; Ibn ʿAmir and the Syrians read ذو agreeing with الاسم, also in the first occurrence, while Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud read ذي in both places.
[TABRISI:55:62-78#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet taught people to keep invoking God as “Possessor of Majesty and Honor.”
[TABRISI:55:62-78/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn ʿAmir reads dhū al-jalāl in the nominative; the other readers read dhī in the genitive.
[TABRISI:55:62-78/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | reports | With the genitive reading, dhī is an adjective modifying rabbak.
[TABRISI:55:62-78/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿud is reported to read “your Lord’s face, possessor of majesty and honor,” with both instances in the genitive.
[TABRISI:55:62-78/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿi says jalāl is used only of God, supporting the genitive reading, though the source counters with poetry using it of others.
[TABRISI:55:62-78/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن جني | reports | For the nominative reading, Ibn Jinni says the word is coordinated with the noun.
[TABRISI:55:72-78/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Tabāraka means that the Lord’s name is exalted and high, since God alone deserves attributes such as being eternal, deity, self-powerful, self-knowing, and living.
[TABRISI:55:72-78/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Dhū al-jalāl means possessing greatness and majesty.
[TABRISI:55:72-78/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan explains al-ikrām as God honoring the people of His religion and allegiance.
[TABRISI:55:72-78/r17] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another interpretation finds abundant blessing in the Lord’s name and urges seeking blessing in everything by mentioning it.
[TABRISI:55:72-78/r18] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another interpretation treats “name” as an added expression for the meaning “may your Lord be blessed,” illustrated with a line by Labid.
[TABRISI:55:72-78/r19] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another interpretation says God’s name is free of every evil and that He has the most beautiful names.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p129/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | One view treats the word name as an added expression, so the meaning is that your Lord is blessed.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p129/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari treats name as integral: the form means blessing is obtained and acquired by mentioning God's name.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p129/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The commentary refers to earlier explanations of tabaraka at 7:54 and dhu al-jalal wa-l-ikram at 55:27. | mentions 7:54, 55:27
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p129/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn Amir reads dhu al-jalal in the nominative, matching Syrian codices; the other readers and the Hijazi and Iraqi codices have dhi, while all agree on dhu at the earlier occurrence.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The common view treats ‘name’ as redundant, like ‘face’ in the prior verse, supported by other Qur’anic uses of tabāraka without ‘name.’ | mentions 55:27, 23:14, 67:1
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Alternatively, the name itself is blessed: if tabāraka means exalted, elevation of the name points to still greater elevation of its bearer, as royal protocol shows.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | If tabāraka means that goodness remains with God, invoking His name removes evil, drives Satan away, increases good, and draws happiness near.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | If it means that God’s name endures, it points to the continued remembrance of God by paradise’s inhabitants.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The common reading here is ذي الجلال, while 55:27 reads ذو الجلال: glory belongs to the Lord, and the name is distinct from its bearer, whereas the Lord’s face is the Lord. | mentions 55:27
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Calling the surviving entity ‘the Lord’ might imply He remains as Lord with a subject; saying ‘His face’ removes that implication and asserts the Real’s absolute permanence. | mentions 55:27
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The closing pairing sets the world’s favors against the afterlife’s: only God is self-subsistent, while the world perishes and the hereafter lasts only because God preserves it. | mentions 55:27
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In that afterlife no name but God’s remains on people’s tongues; they have no need of one another and fear no one, and their conversations invoke God.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The surahs end by naming God: after al-Qamar’s ‘Sovereign, Powerful,’ this surah says remembrance of God is the highest favor and most complete pleasure. | mentions 54:55
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The next surah similarly closes with glorification of God after mentioning spirit, fragrance, and a garden of delight. | mentions 56:89, 56:96

[QURTUBI-FULL:55:76-78#2/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The other readers use genitive ذي as an adjective of “your Lord”; the phrase points back to al-Raḥmān, the name opening the sura.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:76-78#2/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The sura recounts creation by mercy, divine governance, the Resurrection, Hell, and Paradise, then praises the name al-Raḥmān as the source of creation and mercy; God is majestic in Himself and generous in His acts.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:76-78#2/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | All readers agree on the nominative adjective-form at the opening; Qurṭubī takes it to signal the divine Face that believers will see and joyfully meet.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:55:71-78/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | God’s name is exalted because it applies to His essence; if the name is exalted, the essence is all the more so.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:55:71-78/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, ism means attribute, or it is an extra word, as in the cited line about the greeting of peace after a year.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:55:78/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn ʿĀmir reads dhū in the nominative as an adjective of the word ism.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:55:78/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A prophetic report says that whoever recites Sūrat al-Raḥmān has fulfilled gratitude for God’s blessings.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p205#21/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The descriptive phrase dhul-jalal is read in the Syrian tradition as an adjective of the name.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p205#21/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | God's majesty and generosity are bestowed on His faithful servants through His beneficence.

[NASAFI-FULL:v4p205#21/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The refrain occurs thirty-one times: eight follow signs of creation and the beginning and end of creation, seven follow descriptions of Hell and its terrors, then eight describe each of two pairs of gardens.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p205#21/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The eight initial refrains are tied to the gates of Paradise and Hell: one who believes them and acts accordingly has Paradise's gates opened and Hell's closed.
[QASHANI:55:76-78/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The blessed name of the Lord is the Supreme Name by which seekers rise from beginning to end until they attain it.
[QASHANI:55:76-78/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | For lovers who subsist after annihilation, majesty appears as beauty and beauty as majesty without either veiling the other; earlier, they veiled each other before realized divine existence and return to the attributes.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p53/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الخليل | reports | He defines العبقري as anything noble and precious among people or other things; الجلال means greatness, illustrated by an anonymous poem.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p72/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | Most readers make dhu al-jalāl an adjective for rabb; Ibn ʿĀmir and the Syrians make dhaw an adjective for the name, with further variant forms transmitted.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p72/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Here al-ism means the named entity; another view treats the word name as redundant, as face may be in the verse about the Lord's face. | mentions 55:27
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p72/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Blessing can be predicated of the name as elevation; if the name is elevated, the named Lord is all the more worthy of elevation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p72/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The ending of worldly blessings with the enduring face matches the end of afterlife blessings with the blessed name: permanence suits the world's passing, while growth suits the increase and duration of Paradise's gifts.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p72/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The Prophet taught people to invoke God by the name dhu al-jalāl wa-l-ikrām.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p510/r9] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir says both glosses are close: continual remembrance, adherence, and insistence.
